mainTopic: Why offerings slaughtered שלא לשמן are kosher but do not count for the owner, and how we know this for an אשם
overview: The amud opens by finishing why the תורה needed two פסוקים, ״זאת התורה״ and ״מוצא שפתיך״, to teach that an offering brought שלא לשמן is kosher but does not count for its owner. ריש לקיש then challenges this rule: if such an offering is kosher, it should count, and if it does not count, why bring it? רבי אלעזר points to offerings brought after the owner's death, like a woman's עולה, which are kosher but do not atone. ריש לקיש agrees about an עולה but asks about an אשם, which is never brought after death. He rejects רבי אלעזר's reply from רבי אליעזר's opinion and answers himself from ״מוצא שפתיך״. Later אמוראים question this answer, and אביי explains that ריש לקיש's real source is ״ושחט אותה לחטאת״: only a חטאת becomes פסול. To show that an אשם also does not count for its owner, אביי builds a קל וחומר from an עולה. The גמרא then defends it step by step using שלמים, a הצד השוה, and finally a תודה.

steps.title: Why both verses are needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes explaining why the תורה wrote both ״זאת התורה״ and ״מוצא שפתיך״. Each פסוק alone would leave us with a wrong or incomplete idea.
steps.simpleTranslation: With only one פסוק, we would not know in what way the rule applies, so רחמנא wrote ״זאת התורה״. And if רחמנא had written only ״זאת התורה״, I would have thought offerings brought for the wrong purpose are disqualified, so רחמנא wrote ״מוצא שפתיך״.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its explanation of why two separate פסוקים are needed. Each one fixes a mistake we would make if we only had the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With only one פסוק, we would know there is a requirement but not what it applies to. ״זאת התורה״ compares all offerings to a שלמים, which must be brought for its proper purpose. But that comparison alone could make us think a wrong-purpose offering is פסול. So ״מוצא שפתיך״ teaches that it is still kosher, even though it does not count for the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Merciful One', meaning God, the Author of the תורה
'This is the law', the פסוק that groups all the offerings together
'I would have said', an early, mistaken assumption
'Let them be disqualified'
'That which goes out of your lips', the פסוק about keeping your vow

steps.whatToRemember: Two פסוקים work together. ״זאת התורה״ says an offering should be brought for its proper purpose. ״מוצא שפתיך״ says that if it was not, the offering is still kosher, but it does not count for the owner.

phrases.english: one would not know in what [way the rule applies];
[therefore] the Merciful One wrote: 'This is the law.'
And if the Merciful One had written only 'This is the law' —
I would have said that they should be disqualified;
[therefore] the Merciful One wrote: 'That which goes out of your lips.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא ״זֹאת הַתּוֹרָה״ – הֲוָה אָמֵינָא לִיפַּסְלוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the explanation, begun before this section, of why both פסוקים are necessary.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that each verse is needed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With only ״זאת התורה״, an offering brought שלא לשמן would be פסול.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both verses are needed: the offering should be brought for its proper purpose, but if it was not, it is still kosher.

steps.title: Kosher but not counting: how can that be?
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש challenges the whole idea. An offering that is kosher should count for the owner, and an offering that does not count should not be brought at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש lay on his stomach in the study hall and raised a difficulty: If these offerings are kosher, let them atone! And if they do not atone, why are they brought?
steps.whatsHappening: A new discussion begins. ריש לקיש attacks the idea that a שלא לשמן offering is kosher but does not count for the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש sees a contradiction in the הלכה. 'Kosher' should mean the offering does its job, which is to bring כפרה or fulfill the owner's obligation. If it cannot do its job, there seems to be no point in offering it on the מזבח.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'threw himself on his innards', meaning he lay face down
The study hall
Raised a difficulty
Kosher, valid
Atone, or 'gain acceptance' for the owner

steps.whyThisMatters: This question sets up the rest of the סוגיא. Each answer has to show that an offering can be kosher and still not count for its owner.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish lay on his stomach
in the study hall, and raised a difficulty:
If they are kosher, let them atone!
phrases.notes: 'They' means offerings slaughtered for the wrong purpose, the case being discussed.

phrases.english: And if they do not atone, why are they brought?

steps.triggerLanguage: רְמֵי רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ עַל מְעוֹהִי בֵּי מִדְרְשָׁא, וּמַקְשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion that a שלא לשמן offering is kosher yet does not count for the owner.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that offerings brought שלא לשמן are kosher but do not fulfill the owner's obligation
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being kosher and bringing atonement should go together. An offering that is kosher should atone, and one that doesn't atone has no reason to be brought.

steps.title: Precedent: offerings brought after the owner's death
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר answers that we already know of offerings that are kosher but do not atone. These are offerings brought after the owner has died.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said to him: We have found, with offerings brought after the owner's death, that they are kosher and yet do not atone.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers ריש לקיש by pointing to a known case where an offering is kosher but does not atone. He then brings a source for it, in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the owner has died, there is no one left who needs atonement. Yet some of these offerings are still brought. So 'kosher' and 'atones' are not the same thing, and ריש לקיש's assumption is broken.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We have found', introducing an existing example
After death, meaning after the owner has died

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said to him:
phrases.notes: Some versions say אליעזר, in round brackets, but the corrected wording, in square brackets, is אלעזר.

phrases.english: We have found, with those brought after death,
that they are kosher but do not atone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי (אֱלִיעֶזֶר) [אֶלְעָזָר]: מָצִינוּ בְּבָאִין לְאַחַר מִיתָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers ריש לקיש's challenge with a precedent.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A precedent showing the two ideas can be separated
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any offering that is kosher must also atone.
steps.terutzMaskana: An offering can be kosher without atoning, as we see with offerings brought after the owner's death.

steps.title: The source: a woman's offerings after her death
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר proves his point from a משנה. If a woman dies after bringing her חטאת, her heirs still bring her עולה.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: A woman who brought her חטאת and then died, her heirs bring her עולה. If she brought her עולה and then died, her heirs do not bring her חטאת.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר quotes a משנה to back up his claim that some offerings are brought after the owner dies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heirs bring the woman's עולה even though she is no longer alive to gain atonement from it. This shows an עולה can be kosher and brought without atoning. Her חטאת is not brought after her death, because a חטאת is only brought for atonement.

keyTerms.meaning: Sin offering
Burnt offering, burned entirely on the מזבח
Heirs

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the משנה treats both offerings the same. The עולה is brought after death and the חטאת is not. That difference is exactly what ריש לקיש picks up on next.

phrases.english: As we learned [in a Mishnah]:
A woman who brought her sin offering and then died —
phrases.notes: This is a woman after childbirth, who has to bring both a חטאת and an עולה.

phrases.english: the heirs shall bring her burnt offering.
[If she brought] her burnt offering and then died —
the heirs shall not bring her sin offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the משנה source for רבי אלעזר's precedent.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that some offerings are kosher yet do not atone
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in קנים: a woman's heirs bring her עולה after her death.

steps.title: That works for an עולה, but what about an אשם?
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש accepts the answer for an עולה. But an אשם is never brought after the owner's death, so where do we learn that an אשם can be kosher without atoning?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I agree with you about an עולה, since it is brought after death. But an אשם, which is not brought after death, how do we know it?
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש accepts the proof for an עולה but says it does not cover an אשם. He challenges רבי אלעזר to find a source for that case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof worked because an עולה can be brought with no owner to atone for. An אשם exists only to bring atonement, so it is never brought after death. That means the precedent does not show an אשם can be kosher without atoning, yet the הלכה says an אשם brought שלא לשמן is kosher.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I agree with you'
Guilt offering, brought for atonement
'From where do we know?', a request for a source

steps.whyThisMatters: This sharpens ריש לקיש's question. The answer has to work even for an offering whose only purpose is atonement.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is ריש לקיש answering רבי אלעזר.

phrases.english: I agree with you regarding a burnt offering,
since it is brought after death;
[but] a guilt offering, which is not brought after death —
from where do we know [it]?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מוֹדֵינָא לָךְ בְּעוֹלָה, דְּאָתְיָא לְאַחַר מִיתָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the proof for an עולה but challenges whether it covers an אשם.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's precedent from offerings brought after death
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The precedent only covers offerings that can exist without an owner to atone for. An אשם is never brought after death, so it remains unexplained.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר points to רבי אליעזר's opinion
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר tells ריש לקיש that his view about the אשם is already written in the משנה. It is the opinion of רבי אליעזר, who says an אשם slaughtered for the wrong purpose is also פסול.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said to him: your side of the argument is right next to it in the משנה. רבי אליעזר says: the אשם too is פסול.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers ריש לקיש's question about the אשם. He says ריש לקיש's view is really a known opinion in the משנה, the view of רבי אליעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש asked how an אשם can be kosher without counting for the owner. רבי אלעזר does not deny the question. Instead he says the question just shows that ריש לקיש holds like רבי אליעזר, who says an אשם slaughtered for the wrong purpose is פסול.

keyTerms.meaning: Your side of the argument (your opinion in a dispute)
Next to it, right beside it
Guilt offering

phrases.english: He said to him: Behold, your side of the dispute is next to it –
Rabbi Eliezer says: The guilt offering too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers ריש לקיש's question about the אשם from step 5
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributes the questioner's view to a known תנא (the question fits one side of a dispute)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ריש לקיש's logic seems to disprove the whole idea that an אשם can be kosher without counting for the owner
steps.terutzMaskana: That logic is simply the opinion of רבי אליעזר, who holds the אשם is פסול

steps.title: ריש לקיש rejects the answer
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש is surprised and rejects the answer. He was asking on the main, unnamed opinion of the משנה, so pointing to רבי אליעזר's minority view does not help.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: Is this the one people call a great man? I am talking about the main opinion of the משנה, and you answer me with רבי אליעזר?!
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש pushes back sharply on רבי אלעזר's answer. He says it misses the point of his question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The main opinion in the משנה holds that an אשם slaughtered for the wrong purpose is kosher. ריש לקיש wants to know the source for that opinion. Saying that רבי אליעזר disagrees does not explain where the main opinion gets its rule.

keyTerms.meaning: A great man (a great scholar)
The whole משנה, meaning its main, unnamed opinion

phrases.english: He said: Is this the one about whom people say
he is a great man?!
I am speaking about the whole משנה,
phrases.notes: He means the main opinion of the משנה, the one with no name attached to it.

phrases.english: and you tell me Rabbi Eliezer?!

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶהוּ שֶׁאוֹמְרִין עָלָיו אָדָם גָּדוֹל הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבי אלעזר's answer from step 6
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole answer of step 6
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The answer explains only the minority view. The question was about the source for the main opinion, which holds the אשם is kosher.

steps.title: ריש לקיש answers his own question
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש opens his own answer, using the דרשה from ״מוצא שפתיך״. The פסוק calls the offering a נדר and also a נדבה. This teaches that an offering can be kosher even when it does not count for the owner's obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: Instead, ריש לקיש said: I will open an answer for myself. ״מוצא שפתיך״ — is this a נדבה? It is a נדר! And so on, as explained earlier.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש now answers his own question about the אשם. He uses the same פסוק and דרשה the גמרא used earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק speaks of a vow, yet calls it a gift. This shows that an offering that fails to fulfill its owner's obligation is still kosher, like a gift offering. ריש לקיש uses this to teach that an אשם can also be kosher without atoning.

keyTerms.meaning: I will open an opening, meaning I will offer an answer
For myself
A vow offering that a person obligates himself to bring
A gift offering, a specific animal pledged freely
As stated above

phrases.english: Rather, Reish Lakish said,
I will open an opening for myself:
“That which has gone out of your lips, etc.” –
Is this a gift offering?! It is a vow!
And so on, as above.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אֶפְתַּח אֲנָא פִּתְחָא לְנַפְשַׁאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting רבי אלעזר's answer, ריש לקיש gives his own answer to the question of step 5
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings a פסוק as the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: No source shows that an אשם can be kosher without atoning
steps.terutzMaskana: ״מוצא שפתיך״ teaches that an offering can be kosher even when it does not count for the owner

steps.title: Later אמוראים question ריש לקיש's answer
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא, רבי יצחק בר אבא and אביי sit together and question ריש לקיש's answer. The פסוק talks only about vow and gift offerings. Perhaps those are brought without atoning, but an אשם should not be brought at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא and רבי יצחק בר אבא were sitting, and אביי was sitting with them. They said: ריש לקיש had a problem with the אשם, which is never brought after death, and he answered it with ״מוצא שפתיך״. But say that offerings brought as a נדר or נדבה are brought without atoning, while an אשם is not brought at all!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא first sets the scene: three אמוראים sitting together and discussing. Then they challenge how ריש לקיש's פסוק helps with the אשם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש's source speaks about voluntary offerings, a vow and a gift. An אשם is an obligation, not a voluntary offering. So the פסוק might teach only about voluntary offerings and leave the אשם as פסול.

keyTerms.meaning: Was sitting
Next to them, with them
He brought a source (a דרשה) for it
Let it be brought but not atone
After death (after the owner dies)

steps.confusionAlert: These three אמוראים are not arguing that ריש לקיש's original question was wrong. They are asking whether his own answer really covers the אשם.

phrases.aramaic: יָתֵיב רַבִּי זֵירָא וְרַבִּי יִצְחָק בַּר אַבָּא,
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Abba were sitting,
and Abaye was sitting with them,
and they were sitting and saying:
The guilt offering was difficult for Reish Lakish,
since it is not brought after death,
and he brought for it the source “That which has gone out of your lips”;
But say: an offering that comes as a vow or a gift –
let it be brought and not atone,
but a guilt offering – let it not be brought at all!

steps.triggerLanguage: יָתֵיב רַבִּי זֵירָא וְרַבִּי יִצְחָק בַּר אַבָּא וְיָתֵיב אַבָּיֵי גַּבַּיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges ריש לקיש's answer from step 8
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's use of ״מוצא שפתיך״ as a source for the אשם
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק speaks only of voluntary vow and gift offerings. An אשם is an obligation, so the rule may not apply to it, and it may be פסול.

steps.title: אביי reveals ריש לקיש's real starting point
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that ריש לקיש's main source is ״ושחט אותה לחטאת״. Only a חטאת becomes פסול when slaughtered for the wrong purpose, so other offerings, including an אשם, stay kosher. ״מוצא שפתיך״ is added only to teach that they do not count for the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to them: ריש לקיש began from here: "And slaughter it for a sin offering." The word "it" teaches that a sin offering slaughtered for its own sake is kosher, and one slaughtered for a different purpose is invalid. That implies other offerings slaughtered for a different purpose are kosher. You might think they also count for the owner. So the verse says: "That which goes out of your lips."
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question from Step 9. He says ריש לקיש did not rely only on ״מוצא שפתיך״; his real source was a פסוק about the חטאת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ״אותה״ ("it") limits the rule of 'invalid when not for its own sake' to a חטאת alone. So every other offering, including an אשם, stays kosher. ״מוצא שפתיך״ is used only for the second half of the rule: these offerings do not count for the owner's obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: He began, meaning he based his answer on this source
For its own sake, meaning slaughtered for the right purpose
Not for its own sake, meaning slaughtered for a different purpose
All the other offerings
They will count, meaning they are accepted for the owner's obligation

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two parts. ״אותה״ teaches that other offerings are KOSHER. ״מוצא שפתיך״ teaches that they still do NOT COUNT for the owner.

phrases.english: Abaye said to them:
phrases.notes: "Them" means רבי זירא and רבי יצחק בר אבא, the two he was sitting with in Step 9.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish began from here:
"And slaughter it for a sin offering";
"It": when slaughtered for its own sake, it is kosher;
when slaughtered not for its own sake, it is invalid;

phrases.aramaic: הָא שְׁאָר קֳדָשִׁים – שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָן כְּשֵׁרִין.
phrases.english: this implies that other offerings slaughtered not for their own sake are kosher.
You might think they also count for the owner?
So the verse says: "That which goes out of your lips."
phrases.notes: This is the same פסוק from Step 8 (דברים 23:24).

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ אַבָּיֵי, רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מֵהָכָא פְּתַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 9 by showing a broader source behind ריש לקיש's answer.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ריש לקיש relied only on ״מוצא שפתיך״, which speaks only about vow and gift offerings.
steps.terutzMaskana: The kosher status of an אשם comes from ״אותה״, which excludes everything except a חטאת. ״מוצא שפתיך״ only adds that it does not count for the owner.

steps.title: Maybe an אשם does count for its owner
steps.stepSummary: The questioners accept that an אשם is kosher. But ״מוצא שפתיך״ speaks only of vow and gift offerings, so maybe only those fail to count, while an אשם still counts for its owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say this: offerings brought as a vow or a gift are brought but do not count. An אשם, however, should fully count for the owner!
steps.whatsHappening: The questioners attack the second half of אביי's answer. The ״אותה״ part shows that an אשם is kosher, but nothing yet shows that it fails to count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״מוצא שפתיך״ speaks of נדר and נדבה, which are voluntary offerings. An אשם is an obligation, not a gift. So that פסוק may not apply to it, and a kosher אשם could count fully.

keyTerms.meaning: But say, meaning 'why not explain it this way?'
Let it be brought but not count for the owner
It should also fully count for the owner

phrases.english: But say: an offering brought as a vow or a gift
is brought but does not count for the owner,
but an אשם (also)
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some leave it out. The meaning is the same either way.

phrases.english: should also fully count for the owner!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the 'does not count' part of אביי's answer in Step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: Using ״מוצא שפתיך״ to show that an אשם does not count for its owner
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק speaks only of voluntary vow and gift offerings. An אשם is a required offering, so it may count even when slaughtered for the wrong purpose.

steps.title: A קל וחומר from an עולה
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers with a קל וחומר. An עולה does not atone, yet it does not count when slaughtered for the wrong purpose. An אשם does atone, so it is stricter, and surely it does not count either.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: You cannot say an אשם counts, because of a קל וחומר from an עולה. An עולה does not atone, yet it does not count for the owner. An אשם does atone, so isn't it logical that it does not count?!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי defends the rule that an אשם does not count for its owner. He does not use a פסוק here; he uses logic, a קל וחומר from an עולה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already know that an עולה slaughtered for the wrong purpose does not count. An אשם is more serious because it atones for a sin. If the lighter offering does not count, the more serious one should not count either.

keyTerms.meaning: A logical argument: if the lighter case has a strict rule, the more serious case surely has it too
Atones for a sin
Counts, meaning it is accepted for the owner
Isn't it logical?

phrases.english: Abaye said:
You cannot say that an אשם counts for the owner,
because of a kal vachomer from an עולה;
if an עולה, which does not atone,
does not count for the owner,
then an אשם, which does atone,
isn't it logical that it does not count?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: אָשָׁם דְּמִירַצֵּי לָא מָצֵית אָמְרַתְּ, קַל וָחוֹמֶר מֵעוֹלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 11 with logic instead of a פסוק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since ״מוצא שפתיך״ speaks only of gift offerings, an אשם might count for its owner.
steps.terutzMaskana: An אשם is stricter than an עולה because it atones, so it does not count either.

steps.title: An עולה is stricter because it is burned completely
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא breaks the קל וחומר. An עולה has its own stricter feature: it is burned entirely on the altar. So we cannot learn the rule for an אשם from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about an עולה? It is special because it is burned completely!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down אביי's קל וחומר by showing that an עולה is stricter than an אשם in a different way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קל וחומר only works if the first case is truly the lighter one. An עולה is burned completely on the altar, while an אשם is eaten by כהנים. That makes the עולה stricter in one way, so its rule cannot be passed down to an אשם.

keyTerms.meaning: What about...? This is the standard opening for pointing out a difference that breaks a קל וחומר
Completely burned on the altar
Since it is, meaning 'because it has this special feature'

phrases.english: What about an עולה?
It is special, since it is burned completely!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the קל וחומר of Step 12.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The קל וחומר from an עולה to an אשם
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: An עולה is not simply lighter than an אשם. It is stricter because it is completely burned (כליל), so it cannot serve as the lighter case of a קל וחומר.

steps.title: Peace offerings can prove the point instead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 13 by pointing to שלמים. They are not burned entirely, yet they still do not count for the owner when slaughtered שלא לשמן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rescues the proof by switching from עולה to שלמים. שלמים do not have the strict feature of being burned entirely, and they still do not count when slaughtered for the wrong purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge in Step 13 was that עולה is special because it is כליל, fully burned. שלמים are not fully burned, yet the same rule applies to them, so being fully burned is not the reason for the rule. Like an עולה, a שלמים does not atone, so the קל וחומר to אשם can now run from שלמים.

keyTerms.meaning: Peace offerings, mostly eaten by the owners
Will prove it (a case that shows a feature is not the real reason)

phrases.english: Peace offerings will prove it.
phrases.notes: He means: שלמים are not fully burned, and yet they still do not count for the owner when slaughtered for the wrong purpose.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the דחיה of Step 13 by finding a new source that lacks the stricter feature of עולה
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacing the source of the קל וחומר
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule for עולה might come from it being burned entirely, so it cannot teach about אשם
steps.terutzMaskana: שלמים are not burned entirely and still do not count, so the rule does not depend on that feature

steps.title: Peace offerings have their own stricter features
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא breaks the proof from שלמים. שלמים are special because they need נסכים and the waving of the breast and thigh.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about peace offerings? They are special, since they require wine offerings and the waving of the breast and thigh!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from שלמים. It points out that שלמים have strict features that an אשם does not have.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קל וחומר only works if the source case is not stricter in some other way. שלמים need נסכים and תנופה of the חזה ושוק, and an אשם needs neither. So maybe that strictness is why שלמים do not count, and an אשם could still count for its owner.

keyTerms.meaning: What about...? (opening a point that the source case is special)
Wine offerings poured on the altar
Waving, an action done with certain parts of an offering
The breast and the thigh of a שלמים, given to the כהן

phrases.english: What about peace offerings?
They are special, since they require wine offerings
and the waving of the breast and thigh!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the new source offered in Step 14
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The קל וחומר from שלמים alone
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: שלמים have stricter features (נסכים, תנופת חזה ושוק) that אשם lacks, so they cannot teach about אשם

steps.title: Combining burnt and peace offerings into one proof
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that עולה proves the point about שלמים, and שלמים prove it about עולה. What they share is that they are קדשים that stay כשר but do not count when slaughtered שלא לשמן. So the same is true of an אשם.
steps.simpleTranslation: A burnt offering will prove it, and the argument comes back around. This one is not like that one, and that one is not like this one. What they have in common is that they are holy offerings, and if one slaughtered them for the wrong purpose they are kosher but do not count. So I will also bring the guilt offering: it is a holy offering, and if one slaughtered it for the wrong purpose it is kosher but does not count.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא builds a הצד השוה argument. Each offering has its own special feature, but neither feature explains the rule, so the rule must come from what they share, and an אשם shares it too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עולה has no waving of the חזה ושוק, yet it also does not count when slaughtered שלא לשמה, so it answers the challenge against שלמים. שלמים are not fully burned, so they answer the challenge against עולה. Since each special feature is missing in the other case, the rule must come from the shared fact that both are קדשים, which also applies to אשם.

keyTerms.meaning: The argument has come back around to where it started
The feature of this case is not like the feature of that case
The common factor shared by two sources
Count for the owner, fulfill his obligation
Guilt offering

steps.whatToRemember: A הצד השוה proof uses two sources together: each one's special feature is cancelled out by the other, so only what they share is left to explain the rule.

phrases.english: A burnt offering will prove it.
phrases.notes: An עולה has no breast and thigh waving, yet it also does not count when slaughtered for the wrong purpose.

phrases.english: And the argument comes back around.
This one is not like that one,
and that one is not like this one;
what they have in common
is that they are holy offerings,
and if one slaughtered them for the wrong purpose
they are kosher but do not count for the owner;
so I will also bring in the guilt offering,
since it is a holy offering,
and if one slaughtered it for the wrong purpose
it is kosher but does not count for the owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the דחיה of Step 15 by joining עולה and שלמים into a combined proof
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Each source alone has a special feature that might explain the rule
steps.terutzMaskana: Each special feature is missing in the other source, so the rule comes from their shared status as קדשים, which includes אשם

steps.title: Their common factor: both can be public offerings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא breaks the הצד השוה. עולה and שלמים share another special feature: both can be brought by the public, while an אשם is never a public offering.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about their common factor? They are special, since they exist as public offerings!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the combined proof. It finds a stricter feature that עולה and שלמים both share and אשם lacks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A הצד השוה fails if the two sources share a feature that the new case does not have. Both עולה and שלמים can be קרבנות ציבור, offerings of the whole community, but there is no public אשם. So maybe that shared feature is the reason for the rule, and an אשם could still count for its owner.

keyTerms.meaning: It exists as an offering of the public
The public, the whole Jewish community

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying an אשם is not a קודש. It agrees an אשם is a holy offering; it only says the sources have one more shared feature that an אשם lacks, so the proof does not work.

phrases.english: What about their common factor?
They are special, since they exist as public offerings!
phrases.notes: There are public עולות and public שלמים, but there is never a public אשם.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the הצד השוה built in Step 16
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The combined הצד השוה proof from עולה and שלמים
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Both sources share a stricter feature, being brought by the public, that אשם does not have

steps.title: A thanks offering proves the point
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 17 by pointing to תודה. A תודה is never brought by the public, yet it still does not count for its owner when slaughtered שלא לשמה.
steps.simpleTranslation: A thanks offering can prove the point.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new example, a תודה, to answer the challenge from Step 17. The challenge was that עולה and שלמים can be public offerings, while an אשם cannot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A תודה is only ever brought by one person, never by the public, just like an אשם. Still, if it is slaughtered שלא לשמה, it stays כשר but does not count for the owner. So being a public offering is not what causes this rule, and the objection from Step 17 is removed.

keyTerms.meaning: A thanks offering, brought by one person to thank ה׳ for being saved. It is a kind of שלמים that comes with loaves of bread.
'Will prove it.' The גמרא uses this word when it points to a case that shows the rule holds.
A public offering, brought on behalf of the whole community.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the תודה is brought to prove the whole rule by itself. It only answers the one objection about public offerings: it shows the rule also holds for an offering that is never public.

phrases.english: A thanks offering will prove it.
phrases.notes: Nobody brings a תודה for the public. Yet it still doesn't count for the owner when slaughtered for the wrong purpose.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the דחיה of Step 17. That step said עולה and שלמים share the feature of being public offerings, which an אשם lacks.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A תוכיח: brings a new example, the תודה, that lacks the feature the challenge pointed to.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe the rule that קדשים slaughtered שלא לשמן do not count for the owner applies only to kinds of offerings that can be brought by the public.
steps.terutzMaskana: A תודה is never a public offering, yet the rule still applies to it. So the public-offering feature is not the reason, and the rule can be extended to an אשם.
